name: 和菓子 村上 金沢本店 (Wagashi Murakami Kanazawa Honten)

claims.text: Shared confectionery kitchen producing wheat-based sweets (the baked-skin ふくさ餅) alongside other items; no gluten-free protocol documented.
Eat-in menu mixes plant-based wagashi with dairy items (soft serve, mont blanc); no separation or vegan labeling documented.
Some traditional offerings such as mochi with red bean paste and the dry sweet わり氷 are naturally plant-based.

name: 和食ダイニング ばん莱 (Washoku Dining Banrai)

claims.text: The signature aji fry is breaded and deep-fried (wheat batter), and the menu includes sushi and soy-seasoned dishes, so gluten and cross-contact are pervasive.
A sushi and washoku restaurant; standard wheat-containing soy sauce is used and no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned.
Kitchen is seafood-, pork-, and dashi-based; no vegan preparation or separation is documented.

name: 山さん寿司 本店 (Yamasan Sushi Honten)

claims.text: Sushi and kaisen-don are served with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.
An all-seafood sushi and raw-fish kitchen; raw fish and shellfish are handled throughout, so cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable.

name: 洋食屋 グリルニュー狸 (Yoshokuya Grill New Tanuki)

claims.text: Menu is wheat-dominated (panko-fried cutlets, gratin, demi-glace, soy-seasoned fried rice) in a single small kitchen; no gluten-free provision is documented.
The signature yakimeshi is explicitly a soy-sauce-seasoned fried rice (醤油ベース), and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
Core dishes are beef tongue stew, beef-tendon demi-glace, hamburger steak, salmon and chashu — the kitchen is meat- and fish-centered with no documented vegan separation.

The cuisine is built on soy-based ingredients (soy sauce, miso, tofu, yuba), and the sources do not state whether a wheat-free (tamari-style) soy sauce is used. Most Japanese soy sauce and miso contain wheat, so unless confirmed, the seasonings should be assumed to contain gluten. Celiac diners must confirm directly with the restaurant before relying on any dish.

The menu is fully plant-based by Buddhist precept: no meat and no seafood, using only grains, legumes, vegetables, seaweed, tofu and yuba. As shojin-ryori, the dashi is vegetarian (no bonito/fish stock), making it well suited to vegans.
Entirely vegetarian shojin-ryori with no meat or fish anywhere on the menu, so animal cross-contact risk is inherently low.
Seasoning is deliberately kept light to let natural ingredient flavors lead, which can make it easier to identify what is in each dish.

This is not a celiac-safe kitchen. The cuisine leans heavily on wheat: water gyoza are wrapped in wheat dough, and mock-meat items such as the shojin 'unagi' are typically wheat-gluten based. A diner-facing description explicitly states that some dishes contain wheat (and peanut) ingredients.

No gluten-free certification, dedicated gluten-free prep area, or cross-contamination protocol is documented anywhere in the available sources. A truly gluten-sensitive or celiac diner should confirm specific dishes and preparation directly with the staff before ordering.

The menu is soy- and seasoning-forward (soy-milk gyoza broth, tofu nuggets, Taiwanese vegetarian seasonings sold in-house). Most Japanese and Taiwanese soy-based seasonings contain wheat, and no wheat-free or tamari soy sauce is mentioned, so assume soy seasonings here contain wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.

Vegan diners are very well served: the entire menu is plant-based, with no meat, fish, eggs or dairy, and even the five pungent vegetables (onion, garlic, scallion, chives) are excluded, so cross-contact with animal products is a non-issue across the kitchen.
Staff are described as willing to accommodate dietary restrictions, preparing modified versions of dishes or suggesting allergen-free alternatives on request.
Fully vegan menu rooted in Taiwanese shojin cooking, with no animal products at all.
No five pungent vegetables, which also helps diners avoiding onion and garlic.
Staff are open to modifying dishes or recommending alternatives for allergies.

No specific gluten-free protocols or cross-contamination information was found in available sources. The menu is bread- and baked-goods-forward (avocado toast, sandwiches, baguettes, muffins, cakes, banh mi), so anyone needing strict gluten-free should confirm individual ingredients and preparation directly with staff before ordering.
No reviewer comments about vegan cross-contact were found. Note that avocado toast is described as vegan only upon request, so vegan diners should specify their needs when ordering.

Staff generally speak English and accommodate requests; reviewers mentioned being able to request alternative milks (soy milk available for a fee, oat milk also offered) and substitutions such as honey.

Clearly marked and reliably available vegan options, including cauliflower soup, granola, a hummus plate with vegetables, vegan banana-chocolate muffins, beetroot and mushroom vegan sandwiches, and a vegan banh mi.
Plant-based milk alternatives (soy milk for a fee, oat milk) are available for coffee and matcha drinks.
The cafe places particular emphasis on vegetables and vegetarian dishes on its brunch menu, with at least one vegan or vegetarian option always available.

This is contemporary vegan Japanese cooking, which typically relies on soy sauce, miso and amazake-style seasonings. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and there is no documented gluten-free preparation here, so celiac and gluten-sensitive diners should not assume dishes are wheat-free and should confirm each item directly with the kitchen.
The kitchen is fully plant-based and describes itself as serving contemporary vegan Japanese food, so the risk of animal-product cross-contact is inherently low.
Listings recommend telling the staff about your vegan needs and any potential allergies before ordering.
Staff are repeatedly described as friendly and accommodating; one diner reported they kindly offered to make a plate of rice balls with pickled vegetables even after regular service hours.
Fully vegan menu, so all dishes are free of meat, fish, dashi, dairy and egg.
The menu states where ingredients are sourced, which makes it easier to ask about specific components.
Friendly, accommodating staff who are willing to adapt for guests.
